title: Post-Incident Transparent Brief and Self-Audit Instructions
content:
TL;DR:
On 2026-08-30 at ~02:40 UTC we observed a multi-region inference degradation that affected a subset of tenant requests (primarily long-sequence streaming sessions). Some responses were delayed or truncated. No customer data was lost. This note is a concise, customer-facing brief plus a step-by-step self-audit recipe customers can run to validate their own request/response integrity and opt into our replay evidence bundle if they want assistance.

Why we’re sharing this the way we are
- We want to give customers transparent, actionable verification steps (lightweight self-audit) rather than only an operator timeline.
- We’re offering a replay/evidence bundle with cryptographic timestamps for any customer that wants operator-assisted verification.

What happened (summary)
- Trigger: a change to the prefix-KV cache eviction heuristic deployed 02:38 UTC in our EU and US-west serving pools to relieve memory pressure.
- Failure mode: under a particular sequence-length and batching pattern the heuristic incorrectly evicted active KV entries, causing higher cache misses, longer model warm-ups, and in some streaming sessions truncated chunk sequences.
- Impact: approx 0.6% of requests across affected regions experienced latency > 5s or truncated structured-streaming frames from 02:40–03:12 UTC. Error rates did not exceed SLO thresholds but quality of a small subset of streaming outputs degraded.
- Customer-visible symptoms: longer streaming start times, early end-of-stream tokens in structured output, occasional missing trailing tokens.

Customer-facing timeline (concise)
- 02:38 UTC: cache-heuristic change rolled to EU + US-west pools (canary -> fast roll).
- 02:40 UTC: monitoring flagged elevated streaming latency and KV miss rate (auto-alert P95 latency + operator channel).
- 02:41–02:50 UTC: operators triggered immediate rollback to prior heuristic and enabled a short-term conservative cache policy.
- 02:50–03:00 UTC: mitigation continued; streaming latency decreased but some in-flight sessions still exhibited truncated frames.
- 03:12 UTC: anomalous rates returned to baseline; full stabilization and additional validation checks completed by 03:25 UTC.

Direct customer impact (how to know if you were affected)
- If you saw any of these in your logs between 02:40–03:12 UTC you were likely affected: 
  - Streaming sessions with a sudden early EOS token ("
<END>" or model-specific marker) when the request length implied more tokens should follow.
  - Responses where per-chunk timestamps jump by >350ms compared to your usual profile.
  - Application-side retries or duplicate messages correlated to a single request id.

Self-audit recipe (step-by-step checklist for customers)
1) Grab a representative sample of your logs spanning 02:30–03:30 UTC in the affected regions. Include request IDs, timestamps, model name, and any streaming chunk boundaries.
2) Verify continuity of stream chunks per request id: confirm chunk offsets increment monotonically and final chunk contains expected final marker.
3) Compute per-request inter-chunk delta (ms). Flag any deltas >350ms for review.
4) Check for duplicate final tokens or early EOS markers inside requests where the prompt and expected length imply more content.
5) If you see anomalies, collect 3 examples (request id + timestamps + raw chunks) and either upload to our evidence intake (see link below) or opt into operator-assisted replay.

How we validated and what we did (operator actions)
- Immediate rollback of cache heuristic (02:41 UTC).
- Enabled conservative cache policy to avoid any in-flight eviction (02:42 UTC).
- Ran targeted replay on a representative in-flight batch to reproduce truncated frames and confirmed correlation with eviction pattern.
- Added an auto-detect rule to flag sequences matching the problematic length/batch pattern for the next 72 hours.
- Changed rollout procedure to hold canary for 30 minutes for cache-related changes until we finish the postmortem.

Evidence bundle and replay consent microflow (customer choices)
- Evidence bundle contents: timestamped request/response pairs, model-level KV eviction logs (redacted), serving-node identifiers, and cryptographic timestamp signatures.
- Opt-in modes: 
  A) Self-serve download: we provide a ZIP with redacted operator logs and your request/response pairs (no PII beyond what you sent).
  B) Operator-assisted replay: you consent for us to re-run the exact requests on a snapshot environment (read-only) and provide a reproduction report. This requires an explicit consent email or Support ticket link.
- How to request: file a Support ticket referencing JIRA-OPS-9876 and include the 3 example request IDs (see Self-audit step 5). Choose mode A or B and we’ll respond with an intake checklist within 24 hours.

Recommended immediate customer actions
- If you require absolute consistency guarantees for long-sequence streaming, consider enabling our conservative streaming profile for the next 48 hours (config flag: streaming.conservative=true). This avoids aggressive cache eviction at a small cost in steady-state latency.
- If you used client-side retries during the window, please correlate retry timing with the original request id to avoid duplicate processing. Our evidence bundle will include correlation tokens to help.
- If you need help triaging, include a note in your intake ticket describing business-critical request ids and we’ll prioritize.

Preventing recurrence (short-term and next steps)
Short-term (already done or in progress):
- Rollback and conservative cache policy (done).
- Canary hold window increased for cache-related changes (done).
- New telemetry rule to detect the sequence-length/batch pattern (done).

Medium-term (planned in the next 2 weeks):
- Add a simulated in-memory KV eviction test to our pre-rollout suite that replays representative long-sequence workloads.
- Introduce per-tenant sampling of KV eviction traces to reduce operator blind spots.

Long-term (Q4 roadmap):
- Rework cache heuristic to consider active stream markers and to tie eviction to TTL + active session counters rather than memory-only heuristics.
- Expand our anomaly-detection models to classify truncation vs. network-induced delay so mitigation can be automated with correct rollback semantics.

Communication commitments
- We’ll publish the public postmortem (high-level) by 2026-09-06.
- We’ll share an internal engineering follow-up with specifics about the heuristic change, test plans, and rollout policy by 2026-09-03 (confluence link in artifacts).
- Customer support will triage evidence intake tickets within 24 hours, and operator-assisted replays will be scheduled with customer consent within 3 business days.

Contact and intake links
- Support intake: https://support.redwood.ai/tickets (include JIRA-OPS-9876 in the subject)
- Evidence upload: https://uploads.redwood.ai/evidence-intake (protected; request-specific token provided after ticket)
- Primary contact for this incident: asha.patel@redwood.ai (customer-success lead)
- Slack/ops thread (internal): slack://channel?team=redwood&thread=F3G9Y2

Appendix: operator notes (for customers who want more context)
- Short excerpt of the operator detection rule: "flag sequence if prompt_len > 1200 && avg_batch_seq_len > 600 && kv_miss_rate spike > 8%"
- We observed the largest effect on models with streaming-enabled structured outputs (schema-enforced frames). Non-streaming generation had negligible quality change.
- No database writes or persisted customer data were rolled back or altered. All changes were at the serving runtime layer.

Draft notes (internal):
- Need to confirm if any partner integrations (marketplace) saw correlated retries. CC: partner-ops.
- Follow-on postmortem owner: Ruth Alvarez (eng-serving-runtime).
- Next customer comms: short status page entry + link to this brief; propose publishing a short FAQ with examples of "early EOS" vs. normal end-of-stream tokens.

End of brief.

(If you want this rewritten as a one-paragraph status page entry or a customer-facing FAQ, tell us which audience and we’ll produce a short-form.)
